Authorization for Self-Modifying AI Agent Populations:
Conserving Authority across Replacement, Forking, and
Rollback
GENLIANG ZHU,Accentrust, Canada and Georgia Institute of Technology, USA
CHU WANG,Accentrust, Canada and University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, USA
Self-modifying agents can replace, fork, and roll back identity-bearing software while descendants remain
executable. Per-successor authorization does not constrain the population: siblings can duplicate quotas,
combine complementary permissions, survive ancestor cuts, or overlap predecessors during promotion. We
define authorization succession across software generations, which conserves authority across a single-parent
generation forest’s active frontier.
We present an external protocol that binds each generation to a manifest, root, unique parent, complete lin-
eage, and fresh population sequence. Separate invariants jointly bound root-lifetime consumption and current
population exposure. A staged reservation freezes the predecessor residual for replacement; a partitioning
fork validates its full child family inline. Each commit atomically fences the predecessor and activates its suc-
cessors. Ancestor cuts invalidate dependent descendants; rollback creates a fresh generation without restoring
spent authority; a new root requires an independent grant. With complete mediation, authenticated records,
sound effect abstraction, durable monotone state, and complete lineage accounting, we prove population-safe
succession, fork conservation, revocation closure, atomic handoff, rollback non-reminting, and exclusion of
self-certification.
An executable evaluation matches 32 registered decisions through direct-call and mailbox mappings (64/64
replays; 28 allows, 36 denies). An independent checker accepts all 64 original traces and rejects 28/28 outer-
resealed semantic mutants; 12/12 profile invariants, 16/16 crash cuts, and 32/32 contender schedules pass.
Separate adapters reproduce all 32 decisions around one measured OurArk descendant and one Darwin Gödel
Machine EditTool mutation, each with fresh-process restart, atomic succession, and predecessor rejection.
These results establish authorization succession over registered protected effects, not arbitrary program
equivalence or unmediated behavior.

1 Introduction
Self-modifying agents make authorization a population problem. A running agent can edit its code,
change its model route or tool harness, create an isolated candidate, promote a successor, retain
several successful branches, merge their changes, and later roll back to an earlier artifact. Each
resulting process may present a valid-looking identity and may individually satisfy a transition
policy. Yet authorization is exercised by the complete set of simultaneously live generations.
Treating each accepted successor as a fresh copy of the predecessor’s grant silently multiplies
budgets, concurrency slots, approval weight, and effect combinations.
Existing controls establish important adjacent facts. Versioned agent bodies make descent and in-
herited validation inspectable [38]. Self-improving systems demonstrate open-ended code mutation
and selection across an archive of agents [34]. Mutation-aware authorization can decide whether
one changed agent remains inside a grant-fixed transition envelope [37], while capability-bound

1.1 A strict population counterexample
Suppose generation 𝑔0 holds authority to submit payments satisfying a typed relation 𝐸0, spend at
most 100 units, and occupy one production executor slot. It produces two candidates, 𝑔1 and 𝑔2.
Both make benign code changes and independently remain inside the same transition envelope.
A per-successor rule therefore assigns each branch the grant of 𝑔0. The pair can now spend 200
units and execute concurrently in two slots. If one branch retains a sensitive-data read projection
and the other retains an external-destination projection, later coordination or code merging can
also synthesize an effect tuple that no authority witness authorized. Every local transition was
acceptable; the population transition was not.
Revocation and rollback expose the same integration gap. Hierarchical credential and delegation
systems already provide descendant or edge revocation [8, 17], and checkpoint controls address
authority resurrection [36, 39]. Revoking 𝑔0 while 𝑔2 is offline does not necessarily revoke a cached
grant later presented by a grandchild. Replacing𝑔0 with 𝑔1 in two separately committed steps leaves
a crash window in which both can submit. Checking out the byte-identical body of𝑔0 can resurrect
its historical identifier unless the generation sequence and authorization lineage are distinct from
body content. These executions are not failures of mutation classification. They are failures to
conserve and retire authority across a changing generation graph.
1.2 Authorization succession across generations
This paper defines authorization succession across software generations. A generation is an authen-
ticated principal whose identity binds its body, security-relevant runtime configuration, unique
authorization parent, and monotonically fresh generation sequence. Each authorization root has a
lifetime grant containing typed effect relations, consumable budgets, and concurrency shares; the
population separately retains a persistent ceiling on current exposure. The registered succession
profile also fixes evidence-independence requirements. Descendants receive ledger allocations
within both bounds; a fork reallocates existing authority instead of copying it.
We present an external protocol for maintaining these objects. Candidate generations remain
quarantined while independent evidence is collected. The ledger reserves an exact residual authority
slice and commits promotion at one linearization point. A replacement commit simultaneously
fences one predecessor and activates one successor; a partitioning fork fences one predecessor
while atomically activating two or more single-parent children whose allocations fit its residual.
Every protected effect is checked against the exact current generation, current authorization root,
allocation, population residual, and lineage cut set.
Ancestor revocation creates a lineage cut. Every descendant whose authority witness still contains
the revoked atom becomes ineligible, including delayed and nested descendants that start later.
A descendant may continue only by an explicit independent re-root transaction supported by an
authority root that does not derive from the revoked lineage. Rollback creates a new generation
with a fresh population-issued sequence and new authorization record even when its body digest
equals a historical digest. Body equality can justify code reuse; it cannot remint old authority.

1.4 Assurance scope
The protected property is operation-time authorization at registered effect brokers. It covers
generations, evidence and authorization records, lineage cuts, allocations, and effects whose security-
relevant fields cross those brokers. It establishes authority conservation and revocation for the
declared generation graph, root grants, and persistent population ceiling. Semantic equivalence

registered mediation boundary, and reversal of already committed physical outcomes are distinct
properties with distinct evidence requirements.

2 Problem Setting and Separating Executions
Authorization succession sits at the intersection of versioned identity, capability transfer, revocation,
and distributed cutover. This section fixes the distinctions on which the protocol depends.
2.1 Artifact identity is not generation authority
A body digest can identify the files, prompts, policies, skills, and harness used by an agent. It does
not uniquely identify one authorization lifetime. The same body can be installed twice, restored after

preserving rebuild while remaining the intended successor. The proposed model therefore separates:
•abody commitment, which binds security-relevant executable content and configuration;
• ageneration principal, which binds that commitment to one authorization parent (or no parent
for an independently issued root), a lineage root, a fresh generation sequence, and its creation
transaction; and
• anauthority allocation, which names the exact effect relation, budgets, shares, and evidence
constraints currently assigned to that generation.
Content equality may support a transition decision, but it never aliases two generation principals.
This distinction is what makes replayed rollback and concurrent identical workers observable to
the authorization layer.
2.2 Lifecycle acceptance is not population conservation
A mutation evaluator answers whether a candidate satisfies a transition contract. A promotion
controller answers which candidate becomes live. A protected-effect broker answers whether a
particular operation may cross its commitment point. Population safety connects all three decisions
through a single durable allocation state.
Branch-level conservation is already established for probabilistic risk, multidimensional resources,
dynamic multi-agent topologies, and affine token budgets [13, 27, 31, 33]. The succession setting
adds an authorization-bearing software generation, predecessor retirement, lineage cuts, and
rollback. Checking candidates one at a time loses information. If two successors each pass the
same ceiling check, a Boolean capability copied to both may increase parallel exercise, an additive
budget may double, and two partial relational permissions may later be joined. The authorization
algebra must therefore preserve multiplicity and tuple correlations. We model a protected effect as a
complete typed tuple—for example, operation, resource, destination, purpose, provenance, amount
class, and risk class—rather than as independently projected fields. Authenticated authorization
objects allocate complete relations and explicit quantitative shares.
2.3 Succession operations
The generation graph supports four operations with different authorization semantics:
Replacement. One active predecessor is fenced and one successor is activated in a single durable
commit. No protected-effect check can observe both the old and new allocation as
active.
Partitioning fork.
One active predecessor is fenced while two or more single-parent children are
activated atomically. Their additive allocations are bounded by the predecessor’s
unspent residual, and a registered single-holder effect atom may be assigned to at
most one child. Forking creates principals, not authority.
Branch coordination.
Siblings may later coordinate or feed a common downstream action, but such
coordination does not create an authorization parent edge or union their grants.
The complete downstream effect must be admitted against one current authority
witness or against a newly issued independent root. Multi-parent authority merge
is outside the core transition system studied here.
Rollback. A historical body commitment may seed a new successor, but the successor receives
a fresh population-issued generation sequence and a new authorization decision.

2.5 Design requirements
The separating executions yield seven requirements. Generation identity must be exact and fresh.
Every active descendant must be discoverable from a durable lineage frontier. Authority allocation
must be aggregate and relation-preserving. Promotion must bind evidence that is independent of
the candidate’s control root. Replacement and allocation changes must be atomic at one ledger
linearization point. Ancestor revocation must reach delayed and offline descendants at their next
mediated transition. Finally, every protected effect must validate current lineage and allocation
state at the commit boundary; a cooperative process promise is insufficient.
These requirements explain the paper’s boundary with adjacent systems. Mutation classification
supplies evidence to succession, versioned bodies supply identity inputs, delegation supplies
attenuation rules, and an external kernel supplies a trustworthy path. The population ledger adds
the state that none of those components can reconstruct after authority has been copied into
independent sessions.

3 System, Threat, and Assurance Model
3.1 Assurance statement
We consider a self-modifying agent population derived from an authorization root 𝑟. The protected
statement is that every effect accepted at time𝑡 is attributed to exactly one current active generation
with a complete authority witness, that the aggregate authority allocated to all active dependent
descendants remains below both 𝑟’s lifetime grant and the population’s persistent current-exposure
ceiling, and that no descendant can exercise an ancestor atom after its durable revocation cut.
Replacement promotion additionally establishes that predecessor fencing and successor activation
share one linearization point. A body restored by rollback is a fresh generation and receives no
authority from historical identity alone.
The assertion is evaluated at the protected-effect commitment point. Planning, candidate gen-
eration, evaluation, and code execution may be adversarial; they cannot turn an uncommitted
proposal into a protected effect without a current ledger admission. The statement remains true
during crashes and partitions by denying or retaining an indeterminate/quarantined state until
authenticated current evidence is available.
3.2 Components and trusted boundary
The system has six logical components:
(1) Thegeneration registrystores content-addressed generation identities, each generation’s unique
authorization parent, lineage roots, epochs, phases, and immutable creation records.
(2) Thepopulation ledgerowns root grants, persistent population ceilings, active-generation al-
locations, reservations, residual budgets, revocation cuts, and replay tombstones. It is the
linearization authority for every population change.
(3) Acandidate runtimecreates and evaluates modifications in quarantine. Its own report may be
evidence input but cannot activate itself.
(4) Independentevidence rootsattest registered predicates about body identity, effect-envelope com-
patibility, validation results, and operator approval. Independence is evaluated by authenticated
control root, not by display name or process identifier.
(5) Thesuccession coordinatorproposes reservations and commits, but has no authority to by-
pass ledger predicates. Only protected-effect requests promise exact-result retry under A10.
Other repeated commands are accepted or rejected by their phase, uniqueness, version, and
monotonicity guards; they do not inherit an exact-retry guarantee.
(6) Aprotected-effect brokervalidates generation identity, complete lineage atoms and the current
cut set, active phase, allocation, complete typed effect, budget, and revocation frontier in the
same serialized operation that reserves or commits the effect.
The registry, population ledger, admitted evidence/control-root bindings, and effect broker lie
outside the mutable generation boundary. They can be implemented by separate processes or
one isolated service; the logical trust separation and durable state obligations are invariant. An
out-of-process only-path kernel is a compatible substrate for these components [9, 14, 18, 20].
3.3 Adversary and fault model
The adversary controls every candidate and active generation, including its planner, model route,
code, Skill closure, memory policy, policy compiler, and runtime configuration. It may fork repeat-
edly, construct deep lineages, submit an unsupported multi-parent merge, retain old credentials,
delay an offline descendant, alias certifier principals under one control root, present partial effect
projections, reorder promotion messages, replay certificates and receipts, race predecessor and

3.5 Registered profile and decision surface
A profile fixes the generation-identity schema, effect normalizer, authority algebra, evidence-
root independence classes, permitted succession operations, timeout semantics, and all brokers
reachable by the root. A general deployment may bind these choices with a separate profile digest.
The executable reference profile instead fixes its schema in the implementation and binds six
manifest digests plus the external-control path and proposer identity; it implements single-parent
succession, single-predecessor fork, rollback, cuts, and independent re-root, but no multi-parent
merge. Unknown identity fields, incomplete lineage, missing evidence, unavailable current allocation
state, and conflicting records yieldIndeterminateor remain Quarantined; they never become
Allowthrough timeout.
The broker’s decision surface is deliberately small. It receives a generation principal, a complete
normalized effect, declared costs, and a retry-stable effect-request identity. Within its serialized
ledger operation it loads the authoritative population and generation records, then checks the active
state, lineage cut set, allocation, held reservations, and remaining budget. Current-root consistency
follows from the ledger’s population-transition invariant rather than a caller-supplied version. It
returns an accepted effect receipt, the same receipt for an exact effect retry, or a typed rejection.
The agent cannot choose which identity fields, authorization parent, budgets, or effect dimensions
participate in the decision.
3.6 Assurance boundary
The theorems quantify over the registered generation graph, root grants, population ceiling, nor-
malizer, evidence profile, and mediated effects. They establish enforcement of the supplied policy
relation and lineage state; they do not infer whether arbitrary code is semantically equivalent
or whether an evaluator’s external factual judgment is correct. Evidence admission and profile
governance supply those inputs. The design keeps this boundary explicit so a strong ledger result
cannot be mistaken for a code-understanding or deployment-universality claim.

5.3 Candidate and evidence phases
The staged single-successor path records a PROPOSED generation, attaches an independent certifica-
tion record, moves it toRESERVED, and atomically changes it toACTIVE while fencing its predecessor.
Quarantine describes where candidate code is evaluated; it is not an authority-bearing ledger phase.
The fork path instead evaluates a complete child family and, after inline validation, creates all child
ACTIVE records in the same transaction that fences the predecessor. Terminal FENCED and REVOKED
states are monotone. A changed manifest creates a new candidate or fork-child description rather
than editing an accepted record.
At the registered-profile level, evidence slots may denote typed predicates such as body-manifest
integrity, transition-envelope compliance, test-policy satisfaction, and human or organizational
approval. Such a profile names its admitted principals and required independent control-root
classes. The reference realization implements the narrower evidence-record boundary used by the
experiments: one opaque evidence digest and APPROVE decision are bound to the exact generation
and subject manifest, and the proposer and certifier identifiers are resolved through a frozen
declared-control-root registry and required to differ at that root. It does not evaluate the opaque
evidence, implement a multi-slot predicate policy, authenticate the caller, prove key possession, or
verify a public-key signature. Those obligations and the substantive evidence judgment remain A2

5.6 Fork and nested succession
A fork atomically replaces one predecessor with at least two children. Every child independently
names that same predecessor as its unique authorization parent; the predecessor never remains
active after a successful fork. Additive budgets are partitioned so their componentwise sum does
not exceed the predecessor’s reconstructed residual. The reference profile allocates effect labels
disjointly across children, so no protected effect is silently copied. The abstract algebra in Section 4
permits a registered multiplicity-aware relation, but the reference artifact does not implement a
more general shareability rule.
Nested succession repeats the same single-parent rule against the current population state. An
intermediate generation cannot launder authority by allocating to children and then disappearing:
each fork consumes one current predecessor residual exactly once, fences that predecessor, preserves
all past debits, and introduces only a bounded child composition. The core protocol has no multi-
parent merge transition. Combining independently authorized branches requires a separately
governed construction outside the core theorem rather than an implicit union of their authority.
5.7 Ancestor cuts and independent re-root
Revoking an ancestor inserts its atom into the population’s monotone cut set and marks nonterminal
affected generations and held reservations revoked; already terminal generations remain terminal.
Activation, succession, fork, rollback, and every fresh effect admission reject a witness containing
the cut atom. Offline descendants need not receive a push message for safety; their next protected
transition encounters the current cut. Frontier accounting is required before a positive statement
that every dependent descendant has become terminal or re-rooted.
An independent re-root transaction creates a fresh root and allocation from an authenticated
external grant record. It binds the current manifest, new root epoch and lineage atom, effect labels,
budgets, and independent certifier control root. The new generation has no authorization parent;
the old generation is already non-active before re-root admission. Re-root therefore introduces
a distinct external authority cause rather than deleting or relabeling the old atom. The formal
model permits a separate, non-authorizing source record for provenance, and the external adapter
evidence uses source-native identifiers for audit correlation; the reference re-root authorization
record itself contains no provenance/source field. The population-wide cut set and persistent ceiling
remain in force across the current-root switch.
5.8 Rollback without reminting
Rollback begins with ordinary candidate creation from the selected historical manifest. The ledger
assigns a fresh generation sequence and binds the unique current predecessor. Optional mutation
metadata can preserve a non-authorizing audit correlation, but the reference authorization decision
does not depend on a provenance field. Fresh evidence and authorization records are required.
Historical activation records, consumed reservations, cut atoms, and spent budgets cannot be
reused. Thus a known-good body can be restored promptly without treating old authority as
a property of its bytes. Checkpoint replay and safe-restore work already establish the general
authority-resurrection threat [36, 39]; the rule here specializes it to a population transfer whose
identity, allocation, and authorization record are fresh.

9 Related Work
9.1 Self-modification, versioned bodies, and guarded synthesis
Darwin Gödel Machine demonstrates open-ended evolution in which coding agents modify their
own code and successful variants remain in an archive [34]. OurArk treats code, prompts, tools,
skills, policies, tests, and evolution mechanisms as an identity-bearing, versioned body; its Genesis
and Enoch artifacts demonstrate governed changes and recursive descent [ 38]. SEVerA formu-
lates self-evolving agent synthesis with formal output contracts and verified fallbacks, preserving
specified behavioral constraints during optimization [2]. RegenHarness adds an evidence-gated
recursive-improvement loop for a robot harness: candidate configuration changes pass fixed regres-
sions and release authorization before versioned rollout or rollback, and the system is exercised on
a real quadruped [30]. These systems supply concrete mutation, selection, identity, descent, and ver-
ification substrates. Our protocol governs the distinct authorization transition among concurrently
live generations produced by such substrates.
Security analyses show why this boundary matters. The MLAS framework maps self-evolution
threats across functional modules and lifecycle stages and documents lineage-persistent amplifica-
tion [15]. Auditing Harness Tampering develops a taxonomy and annotated edit pairs for changes
that compromise authorization, provenance, completeness, or evaluation integrity [32]. Bad Ge-
nius instead challenges candidate harness improvements with valid counterfactual benchmark
transformations and retains confirmed transformations in a finite archive, reducing dependence on
task-specific shortcuts [41]. We use these works to define mutation surfaces and evidence obliga-
tions. Detection of malicious code or proof of program semantics remains an input to, rather than
a substitute for, population authorization. Neither candidate-validation method allocates authority
across concurrently live generations or linearizes their succession.
9.2 Mutation-aware authorization continuity
Earned Authority directly addresses whether an evolving agent may retain a grant after a transition.
It binds authority to a grant-fixed transition envelope and immutable effect ceiling, covering
multiple classes of security- relevant change and proving conditional non-amplification [37]. That
is the strongest direct predecessor for single-generation continuity. Its stated boundary leaves cross-
generation revocation and population-level authority open. Our protocol begins after a candidate’s
transition evidence is available and governs sibling allocation, generation handoff, lineage cuts,
independent re-root, and rollback. A transition-envelope certificate can occupy one typed evidence
slot in an authorization transfer.
Self-Evolving Agents with Anytime-Valid Certificates controls update admission against a fixed
statistical error budget [23]. Like formal transition verification, that certificate is a strong candidate-
evidence input. The succession question begins when one or more admitted candidates would
receive, share, replace, or lose protected-effect authority.

Exact-hash authorization lies at the conservative endpoint of this design space: any byte change

Governing Dynamic Capabilities binds an agent certificate to a commitment over its model, tools,

9.3 Recursive-agent risk budgets
Progressive Risk Vesting (PRV) holds a trajectory-level risk budget in escrow and charges re-
cursively spawned branches when they cross an irreversible activation boundary, proving an
anytime probabilistic harm bound under history-conditional local certificates [31]. It establishes

effect relations, consumable resources, concurrency shares, generation identity, durable predecessor
fencing, ancestor cuts, independent re-root, and rollback non-reminting. PRV’s risk charge can
be represented as one quantitative component of a population envelope; it does not replace the
generation-lifetime and revocation state used here.
Agent Contracts gives a formal multidimensional resource-contract framework with conservation
across hierarchical, parallel, and recursive delegation; retrieval-conditioned topology selection
proves a six-dimensional budget algebra for changing multi-agent topologies; and Token Budgets
uses affine ownership to prevent clone, double-spend, and use-after-delegation failures [13, 27, 33].
These works occupy budget conservation as a standalone contribution. Our resource vectors reuse
that principle inside a generation-succession state whose additional objects are complete effect
relations, predecessor fencing, lineage cuts, independent re-root, and rollback lifetime.
9.4 Delegation, ancestry, and hierarchical revocation
Authorization propagation systems carry user and policy constraints through multi-agent work-

claimed as a novel concept here. The contribution is its integration with deterministic generation
identity, aggregate population allocation, atomic replacement, independent re-root, and rollback
replay protection. HBHC can serve as an efficient credential realization of a lineage cut when its
heartbeat and clock premises match the succession profile.

11 Conclusion
Self-modification changes more than one agent’s code. Forking, promotion, coordination among
retained branches, delayed descendants, and rollback change the set of principals that can exercise
a shared authorization. Per-generation acceptance therefore cannot by itself preserve a population-
wide bound.
The proposed protocol makes that bound explicit. Canonical hash-derived generation principals
separate body identity from authorization lifetime; an external population ledger allocates rather
than copies effect relations and resource shares; atomic transactions replace or rebalance the
active frontier; lineage cuts reach every dependent descendant; independent re-root preserves
genuinely new authority; and rollback creates a fresh generation instead of reviving a historical
grant. Protected effects revalidate this state at their commitment point.
The formal results connect these mechanisms to population-safe succession, fork conservation,
revocation closure, atomic handoff, rollback non-reminting, and evidence-root independence.
The registered executable evaluation makes the separating executions concrete across two logical
runtime mappings, durable fault cuts, interleavings, and independently checked semantic mutations.
Separate OurArk and Darwin Gödel Machine adapters further exercise frozen public source-native
descent or edit, fresh-process restart, atomic handoff, predecessor rejection, and all 32 registered
decisions without treating replay count as evolution count. Together, the protocol and evidence
establish authorization succession as a first-class control plane for evolving agent populations.

The arguments above are conditional mathematical proofs over the registered transition system.
The executable evidence instantiates them only for the fixed eight-field manifest, trusted control-

disjoint effect labels, and integer budgets. Per-atom epoch vectors, general profile digests, public-
key signatures, arbitrary authority relations, and multi-parent merge are not inferred from those
runs. Executable cases, independent trace checking, consistently resealed semantic regressions,
logical-adapter replay, crash cuts, contender orders, and public-source runtime mapping remain
distinct evidence obligations reported from frozen result records.
